newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters strike, crippling operations at UPS.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters strike, crippling operations at UPS.

text.p: The Teamsters union went on strike at United Parcel Service Monday, crippling operations at the world's largest package delivery company and causing headaches for millions of businesses and consumers.

Striking drivers, package sorters and loaders shut down UPS facilities across the country starting after midnight, hours after a final effort to hammer out a five-year contract collapsed in a dispute over pay, benefits and job security.
The stoppage was the first national strike in the 90-year history of the company, which employs about 300,000 workers in the United States, 185,000 of them Teamsters.

By midday, UPS said only a few thousand union workers had defied Teamster bosses and crossed picket lines while skeleton crews of managers and non-union employees tried to operate the company's massive delivery system.

"There are instances of entire centres, entire operations that are working as normal. But I won't kid you. The overwhelming number of UPS Teamster employees have chosen not to work," UPS spokesman Ken Sternad told a news conference.
Eight striking Teamsters were arrested in Chicago and Boston after allegedly trying to block traffic, police said.

UPS, with $22.4 billion in annual sales, normally handles about 12 million packages a day, or 80 percent of the nation's total, and delivers to corporate offices, small businesses, hospitals and households across the country.
A UPS official in Brussels said it expected the strike to have a limited impact on international traffic.
"Europe has not been affected by the strike. There are no Teamsters here and all 24,000 employees in Europe have been working normally today," said Randy Pulito, the company's European president.

The strike left businesses across the country searching frantically for other ways to ship products and documents, and sent rivals such as the Postal Service and Federal Express Corp. scrambling to service stranded UPS customers.

But President Clinton said the effects were not severe enough to cause him to intervene under federal labour law, which allows the president to step in when labour disputes pose a threat to the nation.
"At this time, I don't think any further action by me is appropriate," Clinton told reporters, noting he had sought intervention by a federal mediator whose efforts proved unsuccessful.
"UPS is a very important company to our country and there are a lot of employees there and I hope they'll go back to the table," Clinton said.

Chief UPS negotiator Dave Murray expressed disappointment over Clinton's remarks but pledged to continue lobbying for new White House action. UPS and administration officials were expected to resume talks on the impact of the strike later on Monday.

Murray also said UPS management was not prepared to budge from its final offer that Teamster officials rejected last week. He called on union leaders to submit the plan to their membership for a vote.
Union leaders blamed UPS for the strike.

"I think working people have been taking it on the chin long enough and I just think working people in this country are saying 'Enough is enough,'" Teamsters President Ron Carey told CNN. "It's a crime that they have forced our members into a strike."
Carey said the union was especially concerned about union work going to subcontractors rather than union workers, as well as pension benefits and health and safety issues.
Union workers walked picket lines or prepared to picket outside about 1,700 UPS hub and shipping facilities and at airports where the company maintains air-delivery operations.
"We're striking for every worker in America. We can't have only low service-industry wages in this country," Randy Walls, a 47-year-old UPS driver, said in Atlanta.
If the strike drags on, its effects could start to ripple through the economy, analysts said.

"We'd probably start seeing some manufacturing shutdowns" if it lasts longer than a few days, said Michael Evans, an economist at Northwestern University's Kellogg School and a consultant for the American Production and Inventory Control Society.
"If this snowballs like that, we could see a substantial short-term dip in the economy."
